st.t: Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
st.an: Shely supports the synthesis’s distinction between ownership reform and permission to practise, portraying Arizona’s ABS regime as regulated experimentation rather than unrestricted deregulation. Her account also reinforces the synthesis’s emphasis on oversight, professional independence and jurisdiction-specific design, although she is more optimistic about investment, technology and the significance of limited discipline and offers little evidence that ABS growth reduces the justice gap.
qs: We did not change the rules and permit non-laws to just start practicing law.

kp.k: Arizona permits nonlawyer ownership through regulated ABS licensing
kp.d: Shely describes Arizona's 2021 elimination of its ethics rule 5.4 and replacement of the ownership prohibition with a detailed Supreme Court licensing regime, informed by foreign jurisdictions. Applicants must disclose and obtain approval for anyone with a 10% or greater economic interest and anyone making firm decisions. She reports 144 licensed ABS firms since 2021, while expressly speaking personally rather than for the court or its ABS committee.
qs: Arizona changed its rules in 2021 to permit non-awyer ownership of an Arizona law firm.
We technically eliminated ethics rule 5.4, which is the rule of professional conduct that says lawyers can't share legal fees with non- lawyers and lawyers can't partner with non- lawyers.
everybody who has a 10% or greater economic interest in the firm or anybody who's going to be a decision maker in the firm
I'm not speaking for the court. I'm not speaking for the ABS committee.

kp.k: ABS purposes include investment, multidisciplinary services, and employee ownership
kp.d: Shely says June 2025 application changes require firms to explain their purpose alongside meeting regulatory objectives. Recognised purposes include capitalisation, collaboration with other professionals, succession through nonlawyer family ownership, and rewarding long-serving administrators or employees. She reports multidisciplinary partnerships and a couple of firms creating ESOPs, illustrating ownership changes beyond private-equity acquisition.
qs: June of 2025, our Arizona Supreme Court added another thing that you have to disclose on the application.
Are you doing this to provide more capitalization to a law firm?
We have some ABS's that have other professionals like patent agents or accountants or sociologists or social workers as their part or financial planners
We even have a couple that have created esops so that some of their individual employees can actually buy ownership into the firm.

kp.k: Technology partners offer potential efficiency across practice areas
kp.d: Shely reports technologists joining ABS firms as partners, contributing generative AI and online-system expertise in estate planning, family law, immigration, IP, and other practices. She regards this as an exciting efficiency mechanism and later says she thinks technologist interest is increasing. These are practitioner observations and expectations, not quantified findings about AI productivity or staffing effects.
qs: We're seeing a lot of technologists come in as partners because they've got some great ideas
whether it's generative AI or just simply online systems that can make firms and lawyers more efficient.
not just in personal injury or mass, but in estate planning, in family law, in immigration, in IP.
I would say just as an aside, I think I'm seeing more interest from technologists

kp.k: ABS ownership does not authorise nonlawyers to practise law
kp.d: Shely stresses that ABS entities must actually deliver legal services, rather than serve as referral vehicles or fronts for firms elsewhere. She says mass-tort applicants and investors have had to recognise expectations that Arizona lawyers undertake the work. In response to concerns about KPMG and accounting firms, she distinguishes nonlawyer ownership from legal practice by Arizona lawyers; she also cautions that generative-AI form creation alone will not obtain licensing.
qs: An ABS law firm is a law firm. It needs to actually practice law. It is not a referral service.
we were serious when we said we expected to see the Arizona lawyer practicing law and that the firm has to hire Arizona lawyers.
Arizona lawyers are practicing law in the law firm.
generative AI might be able to create forms, but you're not going to get licensed to have to do that in Arizona.

kp.k: Independent judgment remains protected despite full nonlawyer ownership
kp.d: Shely says a nonlawyer may own 100% of an Arizona ABS, while the compliance lawyer need not own equity but must have management authority and an employment or independent-contractor relationship. She acknowledges instances of owners attempting to control legal decisions. Experienced compliance lawyers are intended to resist interference, including directions about depositions or settlements, and must report suspected ethics or ABS-code violations to regulators.
qs: yes a non- lawyer can own 100% of an Arizona ABS law firm.
The compliance lawyer still does not have to have an ownership interest in the ABS law firm, but they have to have the authority to manage it
I'm aware of some instances where um private equity have have ste or the investors the owners I'll say the non-awyer owners
have tried to step over the line

The compliance lawyer has a specific obligation to report to the state bar and the Arizona Supreme Court if they believe that anything is happening in the ABS law firm that violates either the ethics rules or the code of conduct.

kp.k: Discipline is presented as evidence of functioning oversight
kp.d: Shely interprets two discipline cases over four years as evidence that the regulatory system works, not that nonlawyer ownership is inherently unsafe. She reports that two compliance lawyers and their associated ABS firms were disciplined and placed on probation, with firms continuing to operate and addressing concerns. She identifies improper investor control, referral-only operations, and deficient intake as failure modes, citing an office manager signing clients in one disciplined firm.
qs: in four years, we've only had two discipline cases.
we have had two compliance lawyers and the ABS law firms that they're they're they were associated with disciplined and they're on probation
They're still operating law firms and now they have shown that they are addressing the concerns that were raised in the complaints.
you have to have clients actually speaking with a lawyer or having at least the opportunity to speak with a lawyer about the scope of representation and the fees.

kp.k: Renewals and internal audits impose ongoing compliance obligations
kp.d: Shely describes a move from annual committee renewals to two-year renewals, while annual fees remain payable. June 2025 filing and renewal fee increases are intended to make the programme self-sustaining rather than subsidised by traditional firms. Compliance lawyers must complete internal audits every 6 months, retained for possible complaint investigations or random audits, covering matters including CLE, advertising, and trust accounting.
qs: You still have to pay fees every year, but you file an application every two years.
In June of 2025, the court um increased the filing fees and the renewal fees.
the program is supposed to be self- sustaining so that lawyers in traditional firms aren't having to subsidize it.
the compliance lawyer must every 6 months complete an internal audit form.

kp.k: Virtual operations are allowed but require substantive management
kp.d: Shely says neither Arizona residence for the compliance lawyer nor a brick-and-mortar office is required. Regulators instead question management capacity, lawyer and staff employment, client numbers, and the firm's connection to Arizona. She identifies limits on managing numerous ABS firms as a pending proposal, not an adopted rule. Inactivity could justify refusing renewal for failure to meet regulatory objectives, although she has not seen denial recommended on that basis; inactive licensing is under consideration.
qs: a brickandmortar office is not required.
you don't have to move to Arizona, but you do have to have sufficient time to be able to actually manage the firm
one proposal that is pending, it has not been changed yet in the administrative code.
We don't want to see somebody who is going to be the compliance lawyer for four, five, six, seven firms.
Could we deny a renewal if it looks like the firm has not been operating? Yeah, actually we could because then you're not meeting the regulatory objectives.

kp.k: Reported survival does not establish measured commercial success
kp.d: Shely reports fewer than a half dozen voluntary licence surrenders out of 144 ABS firms, with some firms still developing procedures or software rather than operating. She says renewal discussions generally convey success, but the committee does not ask revenue or client identities: it asks client counts and lawyer employment. Her favourable assessment therefore rests on reported activity and renewal experience rather than disclosed financial-performance measures.

I would say we don't ask you what your revenue is. We don't ask you who your clients are.
how many clients have you had and how many lawyers are you employing?

kp.k: Private-equity concerns motivate transparency rather than blanket exclusion
kp.d: Shely argues that financial pressure and external capital already affect traditional firms, including through litigation funding. Her defence of Arizona is that licensing exposes ownership and control and adds safeguards beyond ordinary professional-conduct rules. She rejects treating investor pressure as unique to ABS firms, while acknowledging the concern and predicting further regulatory reinforcement of lawyer independence.
qs: Private equity is interested in ABS's because they're already doing business litigation funding in lots of other law firms in other states.
At least under our system for licensing ABS law firms, you know who's involved and you know what their control is
We already have financial pressures on lawyers in every type of firm.
because of the sensitivities to lawyers not being directed by equity. We'll see different changes to our code that regulates ABS law firms to reinforce that.

kp.k: Host anticipates investment-led succession and consolidation opportunities
kp.d: Drawing on her capital-raising work, the host reports that fewer capital groups entered ABS ownership than she initially expected. She describes lawyer demand for exits as a driver of investor interest and anticipates acquisition, partnership, and succession opportunities over the next five years. Her claim that AI, ABS ownership, and private equity may pressure older firms to partner or exit is a personal market outlook, not an established outcome or Shely's forecast.

kp.k: Interstate practice remains contested and jurisdiction-specific
kp.d: Shely explicitly labels as her personal view the proposition that only Arizona-admitted lawyers can practise in an Arizona ABS because other state bars would not permit their lawyers to be employed by one. She distinguishes that employment question from temporary out-of-state practice under locally adopted rule 5.5 and admission for particular cases. She criticises pending California restrictions on co-counselling with nonlawyer-owned firms as harmful to consumers and anticompetitive, and offers constitutional objections as her own opinions rather than adjudicated findings.

California has legislation pending that would prohibit California lawyers from co- counseling with a lawyer admitted in another jurisdiction if that lawyer has non-awyer partners.

kp.d: Shely reports Washington beginning a pilot with limited nonlawyer ownership and Puerto Rico adopting a programme starting in 2026 with nonlawyer ownership below 49%, while regulatory implementation remains unsettled. She describes Utah as narrowing its sandbox and distinguishes its permission for some nonlawyers to practise law from Arizona's ownership reform. Her suggestion that financing may hinder Utah is expressly speculative.

kp.k: Access and technology benefits remain anecdotal rather than measured
kp.d: Shely describes programme goals as increasing affordable legal services for Arizona clients and helping the profession. She personally sees benefits from enabling lawyers to invest in technology and expand service delivery, but expressly calls that assessment anecdotal. She regards the programme as evolving, encourages observers to examine public committee meetings, and does not provide measured changes in affordability, unmet legal need, or AI-driven service outcomes.
qs: The goal is to see is this making any difference not just in access to justice in making sure that more affordable legal services are provided to more Arizona clients.
But also to see how's this helping the legal profession in Arizona.

We're learning as we go what works and what doesn't work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Lynda Shely describes generative AI expertise as one component of technology partnerships making Arizona ABS law firms more efficient, while cautioning that AI form creation alone is not a route to ABS licensing.
pts.d: Shely reports technologists entering firms as partners with ideas for improving lawyers' efficiency, explicitly including both generative AI and ordinary online systems. She also says ABS arrangements help lawyers invest in technology to expand their reach and service delivery; that broader claim is about technology generally, not an isolated AI effect. She reports growing interest from technologists and acknowledges that generative AI might create forms, but cautions that applicants will not be licensed simply to do that. Her accompanying regulatory position is that an ABS must actually practise law rather than function merely as a referral service. She does not offer a concrete prediction of AI replacing lawyers, changing staffing ratios or altering fees.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Shely's professional and committee experience, explicitly characterised as anecdotal for technology-enabled service expansion.
pts.d: Shely draws on her experience with Arizona ABS applications and renewals and her service on the Arizona Supreme Court's ABS committee, while stating that she speaks personally rather than for the court or committee. She provides no AI-specific productivity measurements, benchmarks, named implementations or client-outcome data. Her figures on total ABS licences and disciplinary cases concern the regulatory programme overall, not evidence of AI's effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The technology claims describe developments observed by the 2025 interview, four years into Arizona's ABS regime; no specific AI adoption or productivity deadline is given.
pts.d: Shely situates her observations in the regime introduced in 2021. Her forward-looking remarks express uncertainty rather than a quantified AI forecast. Technology-led ABS opportunities remain conditional on operating a genuine law firm, using lawyers to practise law and protecting lawyers' independent professional judgment. Her warning about generative AI form creation qualifies the scope of the opportunity rather than asserting that AI capability itself confers permission to deliver regulated legal services.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified beneficiaries are lawyers and technology partners in Arizona ABS firms, with potential downstream benefits for clients through expanded service delivery.
pts.d: Shely identifies applications across personal injury and mass tort work as well as estate planning, family law, immigration and intellectual property. Technologists can participate as partners, while lawyers may gain efficiency and access to technology investment they could not otherwise afford. She connects the wider programme to more affordable services for Arizona clients, but presents affordability and access to justice as regulatory objectives rather than measured AI-specific outcomes. The account describes lawyer-led, technology-assisted service delivery, not autonomous AI substitution.
